answer: No. Every surface that resolves the leading edge better is a surface pyHyp will not march, and no marching parameter recovers it.

correlations.claim: cell-size jump at the nose/fore seam predicts marching
correlations.detail: separated cleanly on the first 10 observations, then failed 4 of 5 predictions on a held-out test. The jump was collinear with end_scale in the original sample, so it was a proxy, not a cause.

correlations.claim: an absolute floor on surface cell size near 1.6 to 1.9 mm
correlations.detail: marching cases have a minimum nose cell of 1857 to 2650 um and failing cases 617 to 1525 um, with clean separation. The tip_nose cell separates just as cleanly at 794 to 1016 um against 364 to 677 um. The two are collinear because both scale with end_scale, so this is not claimed as a mechanism.
correlations.significance: the floor runs the wrong way: the march fails as cells get smaller, and every route to a resolved leading edge makes them smaller

question: Can the leading-edge wrap be refined on the frozen S6 topology with pyHyp as installed?

what_remains.note: the only cheap option left and the only one not yet attempted; all work so far has been black-box
what_remains.option: Locate the first negative cell by block rather than by parameter search

what_remains.note: invalidates the atlas and every stored mesh identity
what_remains.option: Decouple the nose point count from the trailing-edge base and tip cap

what_remains.note: pyHyp marching outward from a sharply curved nose is the specific thing failing
what_remains.option: Generate the volume mesh with a tool that does not march hyperbolically

what_this_rules_out: Shrinking the nose block so the same cells cover less curve.
Clustering the neighbouring blocks toward the leading edge.
Spending the unused y+ margin on a taller first cell.
Every marching-robustness parameter reachable from the CLI.
